history: Sirius B was found twice — first mathematically, when Friedrich Bessel noticed the Dog Star wobbling across the sky, then through a telescope in 1862 when Alvan Clark tested a new objective and spotted the faint companion. It is a white dwarf: the exposed carbon core of a star that once outshone Sirius itself, now collapsed to an Earth-size ember holding a full solar mass. Squeezed in beside the glare of Sirius A — 10,000 times fainter — the Pup is the classic test of telescope optics, and its orbital dance confirmed that ordinary stars end as degenerate cinders held up not by heat but by quantum pressure.
